parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Briefly describe two phenomena associated with the photoelectric effect that cannot be explained using a wave theory of light.

markscheme_points.text: two from: • frequency below which electrons not ejected • maximum energy of electron depends on frequency • maximum energy of electrons does not depend on intens[itiy] • instantaneous emission of electrons

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking what wave theory predicts - if light is a continuous wave, energy should build up gradually over time and depend on brightness (amplitude). What would that mean for any frequency of light if you wait long enough?

Hint 2: Now contrast that with what is actually seen - think about how the energy of the emitted electrons changes when you change the colour (frequency) versus when you change only the brightness (intensity), and how quickly emission starts.
parts.proper_answer: Any two from: existence of a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted; maximum kinetic energy of electrons depends on frequency, not intensity; emission is instantaneous with no time delay.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Wave Theory Would Expect**
Think of light as a continuous wave spreading energy evenly. A brighter wave carries more energy, so a very bright light of any colour should eventually give an electron enough energy to escape, after a delay while energy builds up. The electron energy should increase with intensity.

Step 2: **What Is Actually Observed**
In reality, if the frequency $f$ is below the threshold frequency $f_0$, no electrons are emitted no matter how intense the light is or how long you wait. Above $f_0$, electrons come out instantly. Also the maximum energy $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$ depends on $f$ alone, while increasing intensity only increases the number of electrons per second, not their energy.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The maximum energy $E_{\text{MAX}}$ of electrons emitted from a metal surface when illuminated by light of wavelength $\lambda$ is given by the expression $$E_{\text{MAX}} = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$$ where $h$ is the Planck constant and $c$ is the speed of light.

parts.label: (b)(i)

markscheme_points.text: ($\lambda_{0}$ is the) threshold wavelength or wavelength corresponding to threshold frequency or maximum wavelength for emission of electrons

hints: Hint 1: Look at the equation and ask when $E_{MAX}$ becomes zero. That limiting case corresponds to a photon with just enough energy to free an electron, so think what $\lambda_0$ must represent in terms of longest wavelength or lowest frequency.
parts.proper_answer: $\lambda_0$ is the threshold (maximum) wavelength for photoelectric emission, corresponding to the threshold frequency.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking To Zero Kinetic Energy**
Set $E_{MAX} = 0$ in $$E_{MAX} = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda_0}\right)$$ This gives $\lambda = \lambda_0$. That is the boundary case where the photon energy $hc/\lambda$ just equals the work function $\Phi = hc/\lambda_0$. Longer wavelength means smaller photon energy, so $\lambda_0$ is the longest wavelength that can still release an electron.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The metal surface in (b) becomes oxidised.
Photoelectric emission is still observed but the work function energy is increased.
On Fig. 10.1, draw a line to show the variation with $\frac{1}{\lambda}$ of $E_{\text{MAX}}$ for the oxidised surface.

markscheme_points.text: straight line, positive gradient, intercept at greater than $2.2 \times$

hints: Hint 1: Think which part of the equation $E_{MAX} = hc(1/\lambda - 1/\lambda_0)$ depends on the metal and which part depends only on universal constants $h$ and $c$.

Hint 2: A larger work function $\Phi = hc/\lambda_0$ means a smaller threshold wavelength $\lambda_0$. Think what that does to the $1/\lambda_0$ intercept and where the new line must start relative to the old one.
parts.proper_answer: Straight line with same gradient $hc$, shifted to the right to give a larger $1/\lambda_0$ intercept (smaller $\lambda_0$).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why Gradient Stays The Same**
The gradient is $hc$, made only of universal constants. Changing the surface to an oxide does not change $h$ or $c$, so the new line must be parallel to the original with the same positive slope.

Step 2: **Why Intercept Moves Right**
Larger work function means $$\Phi = \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$$ is larger, so $\lambda_0$ is smaller and $1/\lambda_0$ is larger. The condition $E_{MAX}=0$ now needs a larger $1/\lambda$ (shorter wavelength, higher photon energy). So draw a parallel straight line starting from the $E_{MAX}=0$ axis at a value greater than $2.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ m}^{-1}$.

parts.label: (b)(ii)1.
hints: Hint 1: On a graph of $E_{MAX}$ against $1/\lambda$, think where $E_{MAX}$ would be zero and how to find that $1/\lambda$ value by extending the straight line back to the horizontal axis.
parts.proper_answer: Extrapolated intercept $1/\lambda_0 \approx 2.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda_0 \approx 4.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ (450 nm).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Finding The Intercept**
$E_{MAX} = 0$ when $1/\lambda = 1/\lambda_0$. So extend the line in Fig. 10.1 backwards to $E_{MAX} = 0$. The intercept on the $1/\lambda$ axis is about $$\frac{1}{\lambda_0} = 2.2 \times 10^{6} \text{ m}^{-1}$$

Step 2: **Inverting To Get Wavelength**
Take the reciprocal: $$\lambda_0 = \frac{1}{2.2 \times 10^{6}} \approx 4.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$$ This is in the blue-violet region of visible light.

parts.label: (b)(ii)2.
key_concepts: unit conversion with $10^{-19}$ J and $10^{6}$ m$^{-1}$
hints: Hint 1: Compare the given equation with $y = mx + c$ where $y$ is $E_{MAX}$ and $x$ is $1/\lambda$. Think what the multiplier of $x$ tells you about the gradient.

Hint 2: Choose two widely separated points on the line in Fig. 10.1 and remember to convert the axis scales ($10^{-19}$ J and $10^{6}$ m$^{-1}$) to full SI units before dividing $\Delta E_{MAX}$ by $\Delta(1/\lambda)$.
Hint 3: Once you have the gradient value, think how to isolate $h$ using $c = 3.0 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and check the unit J s.
parts.proper_answer: Gradient $= hc \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J m}$, so $h = \text{gradient}/c \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identifying Gradient As $hc$**
Rewrite the equation as $$E_{MAX} = (hc)\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}\right) - \frac{hc}{\lambda_0}$$ This is $y = mx + c$ with gradient $$m = hc$$ and negative intercept $-hc/\lambda_0$.

Step 2: **Calculating Gradient From The Graph**
Take e.g. $(2.7 \times 10^{6}, 1.0 \times 10^{-19})$ and $(3.7 \times 10^{6}, 3.0 \times 10^{-19})$. Then $$\text{gradient} = \frac{\Delta E_{MAX}}{\Delta(1/\lambda)} = \frac{(3.0-1.0)\times 10^{-19}}{(3.7-2.7)\times 10^{6}} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-19}}{1.0 \times 10^{6}} \approx 2.0 \times 10^{-25} \text{ J m}$$

Step 3: **Solving For $h$**
Divide by $c$: $$h = \frac{\text{gradient}}{c} = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{-25}}{3.0 \times 10^{8}} \approx 6.7 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$$ This matches the accepted value, confirming the photon model.
